title: Optimize decision briefing - batching & cache tradeoffs with Aurora Inventory
summary: Redwood team walked Aurora through an Optimize-focused decision briefing: batching and prefix/KV cache tradeoffs for their inventory search workload, cost model scenarios, and a suggested pilot path. Security and residency questions surfaced; next steps are a sandbox sim, security packet, and pricing for a 6-week pilot.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-12 15:30 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Ethan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Liam (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood CSM), Raj (Aurora Eng Lead), Sofia (Aurora PM), Derek (Aurora Infra), Anika (Aurora Security), Tom (Aurora SRE)

SUMMARY (auto): quick demo of Redwood Optimize cost-sim and console recommendations, focus on prefix vs KV caching for inventory search, run scenarios and agree pilot scope

[00:00] Ethan (AE): alright everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro round - I'm Ethan Morales, AE on the account. Maya and Liam will run the Optimize walkthrough. Priya's on security & pilot ops.
[00:15] Raj: hey thanks. we pulled the engineering crew, and we really want to see where batching + cache can shave our token spend for autocomplete and long-context lookups - our inventory search hits lots of similar prefixes.
[00:28] Maya (SE): great, that's exactly the workload we planned to model. today we'll show the console's savings decision matrix, run three cost scenarios, and map to an actionable pilot. caveat - some naming might be off in the transcript; Redwood Optimize is the console module.
[00:45] Sofia: quick ask - our P95 current is ~180ms for search API, target is <120ms, and cost per 1M requests is a hard constraint.
[00:53] Ethan: noted. also curious on security check - Anika?
[01:00] Anika: SOC2 is table-stakes, and KMS integration for key lineage is a must, also we need audit logs retained for 12 months.
[01:10] Maya: we cover SOC2, KMS, and configurable audit retention in the private plane - sorry private plane, I mean private control plane - sometimes the transcript messes with "plane" vs "plane"—uh control plane. for hosted we have managed KMS integrations too.
[01:35] Derek: are there any data residency knobs? we need europe-only for some data shards.
[01:40] Liam: yes you can pin region routing policies; the runtime can route by region tiers and fallback - we'll include that in the pilot design.
[02:00] Maya: ok demoing console now — showing savings decision matrix. imagine three rows: low batching (latency-focused), moderate batching with prefix-cache enabled, aggressive batching + KV lookahead.
[02:18] Raj: can you remind me the difference between prefix cache and KV? our search is prefix heavy, but we also have some session lookups.
[02:25] Maya: sure. prefix cache stores outputs for short prompt prefixes — good for autocomplete; KV cache is more general key-value lookahead for repeated long contexts (we call it session/KV), faster for session continuations but needs lookahead indexing and a slightly different TTL strategy. prefix is cheaper to index but less flexible.
[02:50] Raj: hmm okay, so for inventory autocomplete, prefix should be win?
[02:55] Maya: likely. but the cost model depends on hit rates, TTL, and your tokenization pattern. we'll run sims.
[03:10] [screen share noise] Maya: loading the cost sim — first scenario: baseline (no cache, simple concurrency 10). baseline tokens per request ~ 420 on avg from your trace. cost estimate X. P95 latency 170-190ms.
[03:35] Sofia: is that 420 tokens per ingest or per search? our search pipeline includes both prompt + embedding calls.
[03:40] Maya: good call, in our sim we model prompt tokens; embedding calls are separate and we need your numbers. include them in the dataset you share.
[03:52] Maya: scenario two: prefix cache with short TTL (3 seconds) and moderate batch size (batch cap 8). hit rate assumptions 28-35% for your traffic; cost drops ~22% but P95 improves to ~115-125ms.
[04:20] Raj: 22% is promising. what's the risk if hit rate is only 10%?
[04:28] Maya: if hit rate is low, prefix still adds lookup overhead, sometimes increases tail latency slightly under heavy miss storms — we model fallback to streaming and there's an automatic batch bypass threshold.
[04:45] Liam: also note continuous batching has jitter; we pick batch time windows adaptive to keep P95 under SLO while capturing batching gains.
[05:05] Maya: scenario three: KV lookahead with session affinity + larger batching (batch cap 24), assume 60% cacheability for long sessions. cost drop ~45-55% in mid/high QPS, P95 varies 110-140ms depending on routing. but complexity and integration engineering is higher.
[05:30] Derek: integration engineering meaning what? we have to emit keys from our app?
[05:36] Maya: yes you need a KV key strategy, consistent keys for sessions/prefixes, TTL management, and initial dataset ingestion to seed common keys. we provide SDK helpers.
[05:50] Raj: ok length of pilot to validate?
[05:55] Ethan: we typically do 4-6 weeks: week 1 ingest + baseline bench, weeks 2-4 iterate configs and run sims, final week validate metrics and run regression checks.
[06:10] Sofia: what do you need from us to start?
[06:14] Liam: traffic traces (at least 48-72 hours of production-ish), a sample dataset for indexing common prefixes, success criteria (target cost reduction percent and latency target), and infra contacts for sandbox creds.
[06:25] Raj: we'll share traces but need to scrub PII — can you accept redacted traces?
[06:30] Priya: yes redwood sandbox accepts scrubbed traces; we just need timing and token counts intact.
[06:38] Anika: security question - how are logs stored in the sandbox? encrypted at rest? who holds keys?
[06:42] Priya: sandbox uses customer-managed keys in private deployments; hosted sandbox uses Redwood-managed keys but with KMS options for enterprise. will attach docs.
[06:55] [10 min into call] Maya: walking through the console's sensitivity sliders — we can vary batch cap, prefix TTL, and the cache size to produce a savings curve. i'll push to the high-level sim now.
[07:20] Raj: curious on warmup — if cache seeds are missing, how fast does hit rate ramp?
[07:28] Maya: depends on traffic shape; for autocomplete where prefixes repeat a lot, hits ramp within hours; for long-tail lookups, you need intentional seeding or prefetch of top ~10k prefixes.
[07:40] Derek: how heavy is the prefetch bandwidth? we can't load tens of millions.
[07:45] Maya: you don't need millions; for inventory often the head is small — top 10-50k prefixes cover most traffic. prefetching can be incremental.
[07:58] Sofia: can we do hybrid? prefix for autocomplete + KV for sessions?
[08:03] Maya: absolutely — many customers run hybrid. console can simulate layered caches and show marginal gains.
[08:20] Raj: show us an example tradeoff matrix — where do we pick the pilot config?
[08:25] Maya: (shares matrix) we recommend Pilot A: prefix cache + small batch cap (8) as low-risk; Pilot B: prefix + limited KV (session only) as mid-risk; Pilot C: full KV + aggressive batch as high-reward but higher engineering cost. for Aurora Inventory i'd recommend Pilot A first.
[08:50] Raj: prefer low friction — Pilot A sounds right. what's expected uplift in cost per 1M requests?
[08:56] Maya: for your traces, Pilot A model shows ~20-30% unit cost reduction on model tokens; end-to-end cost including infra is approx 15-25% depending on hit rate and embedding calls.
[09:15] Tom (SRE, slightly unclear in transcript): and on the dedicated vs hosted question — if we go dedicated GPUs later, do these caching rules change?
[09:22] Liam: conceptually no, runtime supports same caching semantics across hosted/dedicated/private. on dedicated you may see different batching tolerances because of throughput headroom and lower per-token infra cost.
[09:35] Anika: any compliance gap if we route through multiple regions?
[09:40] Priya: you can pin to eu-west region and Redwood will uphold data residency for the pinned workload. we'll include the routing policy doc.
[09:55] Raj: what about fallback behavior? if cache backend is overloaded?
[10:00] Maya: automatic fallback to model variant or to streaming with backpressure. you can set a fallback policy per route in the console.
[10:12] [10:30] Maya: quick note on metrics — console surfaces token-level spend, cache hit/miss rates, per-route latency percentiles and a delta column for simulated savings if the pilot config were live.
[10:30] Raj: that delta column is key.
[10:38] Maya: showing bench-run example — here's baseline QPS 2k scenario, Pilot A reduces token spend across the run. small transcription glitch: "KV" got read as "K-Vee" in the UI sometimes.
[10:55] Derek: are there rate-limiting or quota implications for prefetching? we need to ensure we don't blow through rate quotas on model endpoints.
[11:00] Liam: prefetches are accounted like requests; we recommend throttled prefetch and incremental seeding; console's sim shows the added token cost.
[11:18] Sofia: pricing ask — can you share ballpark pilot pricing and an optional committed capacity discount if we move to dedicated?
[11:25] Ethan: yes i'll send pilot pricing, and we can model committed capacity discounts — typically committed pricing steps kick in at 3-6 month reserved capacity.
[11:35] Raj: one more technical - TTL sizing: how do you pick prefix TTL?
[11:40] Maya: TTL trades freshness vs hit rate. for autocomplete we often pick 1-5 seconds for very chatty UIs; for inventory lookup where data rarely changes, TTL can be minutes but you must consider stale results. we can set invalidation hooks via pub/sub too.
[11:58] Anika: any encryption-in-transit specifics for KV lookups?
[12:03] Priya: all RPCs are TLS 1.3; for private deployments you can also enable mTLS between your infra and the runtime.
[12:18] [wrap-up portion] Ethan: recap: pilot A (prefix + small batching) recommended, deliverables - pricing, SOC2/KMS docs, sandbox creds, bench scripts. next meeting: bench run planning week — propose 2026-09-16 for a 45-min bench preflight with SREs.
[12:45] Raj: sounds good. minor note - can you include an example prefetch script?
[12:50] Maya: yes will include a sample node/python prefetch example and the SDK helper.
[13:02] Tom: quick interruption - does the console support file-based seed ingest? we've got CSV indexes we can upload.
[13:08] Liam: yes bulk ingest via console or API, we support CSV/NDJSON.
[13:20] Sofia: ok thanks everyone.
[13:25] Ethan: thanks all, we'll follow up with artifacts in the CRM and email.

Transcription notes: occasional mis-attribution (Tom sometimes tagged as "Tom - SRE (uncertain role)"), words like "plane"/"plane" confusion, small ASR errors in product names ("Redwood Optimize" shown as "Redwood Optimizer" in one slide).

End of transcript.
